div.div:
Each tenant's pods get unique IAM roles mapped to
Kubernetes service accounts via OIDC provider,
reducing blast radius and enforcing tenant isolation

path.style: fill: light-dark(rgb(0, 0, 0), rgb(255, 255, 255)); stroke: light-dark(rgb(0, 0, 0), rgb(255, 255, 255));

div.style: display: flex; align-items: unsafe center; justify-content: unsafe center; width: 1px; height: 1px; padding-top: 255px; margin-left: 470px;

div.div:
Prevents “connection storm” crashes,
The app uses AWS IAM to request a
short-lived DB auth token.
RLS (row-level security)
enforces data access rules
inside the database itself by mapping
IAM role--> DB role
and DB role --> RLS policy

div.style: display: flex; align-items: unsafe center; justify-content: unsafe flex-start; width: 1px; height: 1px; padding-top: 435px; margin-left: 337px;
box-sizing: border-box; font-size: 0; text-align: left; color: #000000;
display: inline-block; font-size: 12px; font-family: Helvetica; color: light-dark(#000000, #ffffff); line-height: 1.2; pointer-events: all; font-weight: bold; white-space: nowrap;

div.div:
In this case, the “tenant boundary” is enforced at three layers:
1) Kubernetes namespace/scheduling boundary
2) AWS IAM identity boundary (per-tenant)
3) Database boundary (instance-level OR RLS)

div.div:
